analysis.one_liner: Requires caffeine content labels on foods and 'high caffeine' warnings on chain restaurant menus.
analysis.headline: A caffeine-labeling bill with 16 bipartisan cosponsors was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in March 2025 and has seen no committee vote or floor action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any food, drink, or supplement with more than 10 milligrams of caffeine to state on the label how much caffeine it contains, whether that caffeine is added or natural, and that the recommended daily limit for healthy adults is 400 milligrams. Chain restaurants with 20 or more locations would have to mark menu items with 150 or more milligrams of added caffeine as 'High caffeine' and list caffeine milligrams in writing on request. It also orders the FDA to re-examine whether caffeine should keep its 'generally recognized as safe' status, directs NIH to study caffeine's effects on children, pregnant women, and people with heart conditions, and requires a government study of how caffeinated drinks are marketed to kids.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially people with heart conditions, pregnant and breastfeeding women, parents of teenagers, and anyone who drinks caffeinated products without knowing how much caffeine they contain. Today most products do not list caffeine amounts at all, even though many popular energy and coffee drinks contain several hundred milligrams per serving.

how_it_helps.text: Any food or supplement with more than 10 milligrams of caffeine must state the milligrams of caffeine, whether the caffeine is added or naturally occurring, and the 400-milligram daily recommended limit for healthy adults [S2][S3].

Restaurant chains with 20 or more locations must place a 'High caffeine' statement next to any menu item with 150 or more milligrams of added caffeine, and expand the written nutrition information they provide to include caffeine content [S2][S3].

The FDA must review the safety of caffeine and other stimulants, including guarana and taurine blends, and decide whether caffeine should remain 'generally recognized as safe'; NIH must review caffeine's effects on children, people with heart conditions, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups [S2][S3].
The Government Accountability Office must study how caffeinated beverages are marketed, including whether marketing is misleading or targeted at children and teens [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Caffeinated beverage and food manufacturers, dietary supplement makers, and large restaurant chains would bear labeling and compliance costs, and would face potential new regulation if the FDA review changes caffeine's safety status. The bill authorizes $2 million in appropriations for the FDA and NIH reviews [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Beverage, supplement, and chain restaurant makers

drawbacks.text: Labeling requirements add compliance costs for food and drink makers and large restaurant chains, costs that can be passed to consumers as slightly higher prices [S3].

Requiring the FDA to re-examine whether caffeine is 'generally recognized as safe' could lead to reformulation or restrictions on widely sold energy drinks and supplements, which industry would oppose [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that a 400-milligram advisory label covers healthy adults only and does not by itself protect the most vulnerable groups, such as people with undiagnosed heart conditions, beyond giving them information [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are cheap and targeted: printing caffeine amounts and a 'High caffeine' flag on menus costs industry little but gives at-risk consumers information they cannot get today, since caffeine is not usually listed even on highly caffeinated products. The costs are modest compliance expenses for manufacturers and restaurants. The main weightier consequence is the FDA safety review, which could produce stricter rules for the energy drink market; whether that is a cost or a benefit depends on what the science finds.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it — no hearing, no vote, no trip to the floor — though this Congress is still in session [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Menendez (D-NJ) introduced the bill on March 31, 2025 with 13 original cosponsors [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction [S5][S1].
It has attracted 16 cosponsors, 15 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].
No committee markup, hearing vote, or floor vote has been recorded since referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, caffeinated beverage and supplement makers and large restaurant chains are better off: no labeling costs, and the FDA's re-examination of caffeine's safety status has not been required.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Beverage and restaurant industries, for now

sides.party_line_note: No votes have been taken; the 16 cosponsors are 15 Democrats and 1 Republican, so early support skews heavily Democratic despite the bill's bipartisan framing.

industries.industry: Energy drink and caffeinated beverage makers
industries.note: The bill would force caffeine content labeling and, more significantly, require the FDA to re-examine whether caffeine's 'generally recognized as safe' status should stand, opening the door to limits or reformulation. Consumers currently cannot tell how much caffeine a drink contains from its label.

Supplements with more than 10 milligrams of caffeine would need content labels and the 400-milligram daily limit advisory, and the FDA review covers stimulant blends like guarana and taurine common in supplements. Some supplements are highly caffeinated with no disclosure.

Chains with 20 or more locations would have to flag menu items with 150 or more milligrams of added caffeine as 'High caffeine' and list caffeine content in writing. The cost is modest but the disclosure directly informs customers about very high-caffeine items.

industries.industry: Naturally caffeinated foods (coffee, tea, chocolate products)
industries.note: These products would also carry caffeine labels including whether caffeine is naturally occurring, a modest compliance burden. The disclosure treats them the same as products with added caffeine, though natural sources are generally easier for consumers to identify.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits where most private-member bills do: awaiting committee action that may never come. With 16 cosponsors and no Energy and Commerce markup scheduled, its likely path, unless the chair schedules a hearing or it gets attached to a larger food-safety package, is to remain pending through the end of the 119th Congress without a vote.
